articles.title: The iPhone Duo's Slick Opening and Closing Animation Has Already Been Reproduced on the Galaxy Fold 8
articles.summary: What's stopping the animation from being implemented throughout Samsung's launcher is that the permissions necessary for that only exist in Android's background processes.
articles.body:
Apple just announced iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, yesterday at its "Suprise and Shine" event. Though the concept of a foldable is new for Apple, it's entering into a vast, existing landscape of folding phones. So of course someone has already recreated the Duo's neat opening animation on an Android phone.

While the iPhone Duo doesn't come out until October 23, one of the more interesting early features shown off has been the Apple A20 Pro's ability to power both displays at the same time. This allows the Duo to have an opening and closing animation that makes it look, at a certain angle, like the phone's display is expanding. The effect is unique to Apple's new phone, but a software developer on Reddit was able to recreate it on a Galaxy Z Fold , though it isn't exactly system wide.

In the video user moomanjohnny shared to the GalaxyFold subreddit, you can see the Galaxy Z Fold 8 's outer display fade out as the phone opens, only to have the inner display take the image of the home screen and expand it once the phone is fully opened. This was done by taking data from the hinge sensor and then creating a transition animation using a screenshot of the homescreen – not exactly ready for system-wide implementation.

What's stopping this from being implemented throughout Samsung's launcher is that the permissions necessary for that only exist in Android's background processes. Later in the thread, moomanjohnny explains, "SystemUI is privileged by the system in the way that it can layer itself on top of apps, and tell other apps how to render. SystemUI receives a list of surfaces and can composite them on the screen where it wants using SurfaceFlinger." That because it's a security risk. "Unfortunately, as far as I'm aware, no vendor has made any of these APIs available to anything other than SystemUI."

It's up in the air whether or not this kind of opening animation will ever be supported on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but it's clear that the hardware capability is there. With how the Samsung Mobile Twitter page threw a fit about the iPhone Duo during Apple's event, it's possible that this functionality will find its way to the Samsung Fold range at some point.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: The Clock Is Ticking to Pull Off an Entirely New ‘60 Minutes’
articles.summary: Led by new EP Nick Bilton, the venerable newsmagazine is expected to have a "banger" of a first episode. Can the show hold it together all season amid the up...
articles.body:
In the early days of CBS News, Edward R. Murrow led programs like Person to Person and See It Now from CBS' Manhattan studios in Grand Central Terminal.

The network would eventually depart Grand Central for the CBS Broadcast Center on West 57th street (what was once the CBS space in the train terminal is now a tennis club), but the network's history in the building is the stuff of news lore.

So it makes some level of sense that when CBS News was contemplating where to stage a correspondent photo for its rebooted 60 Minutes , it would take the elevator downstairs to the Terminal's basement, turning the gilded dining room of the Grand Central Oyster Bar into its studio.

CBS News, led by editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, needs the new 60 Minutes to work. Its success or its failure could define her tenure at the network.

The overhaul was the talk of the business earlier this summer, with its EP and a slew of senior producers exiting, and high-profile correspondents choosing to exit (Anderson Cooper) or unceremoniously shown the door (Scott Pelley, Sharyn Alfonsi, Cecilia Vega).

60 Minutes is the most-watched news program in America, and if it slipped and lost that title in the wake of the overhaul, it would be an embarrassment to the news division.

That may be why CBS is playing it so safe as it prepares to debut its new season this Sunday. In the correspondent photo from the Oyster Bar, it is four familiar faces front and center: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, and Jon Wertheim, as well as Norah O'Donnell, who is moving from a contributor to a correspondent. The other new correspondents, as well as new EP Nick Bilton, are off to either side.

The inaugural trailer, which features the tagline "It's Time," features those four correspondents front and center too, providing familiar faces to viewers.

On Wednesday, video billboards began to play in Times Square on the outside of Paramount's building, ending with the quote "It's time to see for yourself," as if daring viewers to see just how radically different… or not… the show is.

"I'm sure the first Sunday will be a banger. Shows three, four, and five could get quite interesting, I think," says Wendy McMahon, the former president of CBS News and Stations, speaking at the Status Summit Wednesday in New York.

McMahon's suggestion, of course, is that the show has been dealt a brain drain since it last debuted new episodes. Enormous effort will be put into the new season, but with so many tenured producers and correspondents out, and so many new names in, it remains to be seen if they will be able to pull off the overhaul this year, or if more seasoning will be required.

"The reality is that there was a lot of institutional knowledge that either walked out or was escorted out the door, and so much of what makes 60 Minutes 60 Minutes is its DNA," McMahon said. "So, am I concerned that the DNA of 60 Minutes is being rewritten in real time? Am I concerned that in the quest to transform, that the problem has been misdiagnosed, and we are potentially changing, dismantling the very thing we are meant to protect? Yes, I am absolutely concerned, but I will stop short of weighing in on the death of 60 Minutes until I see this next 60 Minutes ."

One thing that is clear: The secret sauce of 60 Minutes remains unchanged: It will still have the familiar three segment format, and it will still launch after the NFL late afternoon window, which many in the industry see as the driving force behind its ratings dominance. As THR noted early this year , the show has long been defined by its format and timeslot, and while the correspondents are familiar faces, the show has always been an ensemble, unlike most TV news programs which are star-driven.

As in previous years, one of the segments (likely the first one, if history is a guide) will be sports-related, in this case a feature on the Los Angeles Rams, including an interview with coach Sean McVay. There is also an exclusive interview with the U.S. pilot who was rescued behind enemy lines in Iran, and a third segment yet to be revealed.

They are, to be blunt, completely typical 60 Minutes segments (though the access-driven Pentagon story, including an interview with Secretary Pete Hegseth, is sure to raise eyebrows). Though as McMahon suggested, the first episode will put the show's best face forward. She says she left CBS News in part because "I had enough of an understanding of the plan moving forward for CBS News and for 60 Minutes , and I knew that I could not lead or own that plan, not journalistically, and not from a business strategy perspective."

In fact, many of Bilton's coming "innovations" seem like throwbacks to previous eras of the show. He told THR after his hiring that he wanted to bring some "gonzo journalism" to the show, with The New York Times reporting that hidden camera segments are among those in the works (they used to be used sparingly in the show's distant past). He also teased a new end-of-show segment, and while he was coy on what it is, there had been reports that CBS had approached people like Jerry Seinfeld (whose daughter works at The Free Press), John McEnroe, and Stephen A. Smith about some sort of Andy Rooney-esque commentary segment.

A TV news source speculated that the show may revive the "Point/Counterpoint" debate segment that the show had in the 1970s, with liberal and conservative pundits debating a contentious issue.

But the coming iteration of 60 Minutes has, for better or worse, become culture war fodder, only ramping up the stakes.

Guy Campanile, the show's former managing editor, who was among those shown the door earlier this year by Weiss, wrote on Facebook this week that the team that was ousted "refused to be accomplices in the destruction of the most prestigious news program on American television."

Heavy stuff, though not everyone agreed that Weiss' move to overhaul the show is out of bounds.

Brian Williams, the former NBC Nightly News anchor who briefly hosted a 60 Minutes -esque newsmagazine called Rock Center , said at the Status Summit: "Could 60 Minutes use a new coat of paint? Yep."

"I always found it curious that a news broadcast took the summer off. That dates back to Don Hewitt loving tennis, and he played tennis from Memorial Day to Labor Day, and then they went back to work. Apparently, news stops during those months, so I'd like to see a 52-week-a-year broadcast," he continued. "But you know, talent decisions are talent decisions and ditto producers. We all came to work every day knowing that it could be our last and keeping our resumes fresh. It's a tough business. These jobs still tend to be overpaid. They still tend to be indoor work… So we're all riding the wave."

Even inside CBS News well before David Ellison's takeover of Paramount, the independence of 60 Minutes was seen as a blessing and a curse. The show was the best in its category, but was slower than others to adopt to changing consumer habits, though it was working on some digital initiatives when Weiss took over CBS News.

A former senior executive at CBS said that suggestions from corporate to the show's producers were often brushed aside in the pre-Weiss era, even if they were made in good faith and with what they believed were the best interests of the show in mind.

And while it may seem obvious to many in the industry that shaking up the most-watched news show in America is a crazy move, it is not universally so.

When pressed by Oliver Darcy at the Status Summit about the firing of Pelley, the former NBC News, CNN and CNBC producer Jonathan Wald quipped "you've got to break some eggs to make an omelette," to a couple of gasps from the crowd.

"I have a hugely contrarian view of three things: I'm not afraid of AI necessarily. I'm not really afraid of data centers because I think at some point no one's going to need them. Like, we don't need a giant Texas Instruments calculator. It's all going to shrink, and they'll use them for skate parks or housing or something," Wald said. "And I don't think Bari Weiss is automatically bad for the news business."

But when it comes to 60 Minutes , that ticking clock won't stop. One way or another, the show must go on. CBS News and Paramount executives, meanwhile, are crossing their fingers that those NFL viewers stick around too.

articles.title: The iPhone Duo Might Be One of the First Foldables That's Good for Gaming
articles.body:
I've been hooked on foldables for years now, and I carry the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra on me every day. While that phone is incredible for most of what I need to do on a day-to-day basis, gaming has never felt amazing on it.

A big part of that comes down to the aspect ratio of the larger inner screen. A lot of games will adopt the 4:3 aspect ratio, but there are plenty that just don't, leading to either an ugly, stretched picture or giant black bars. In Hearthstone , for example, I have the choice of having a third of the screen blocked off, or have it stretch out to fill the screen, only to cut off a good portion of what's supposed to be displayed.

There have been several times where I've tried to fullscreen that game, only to not be able to read a card on one of the far edges of the battlefield, because the image is cut off. Now, a lot of this does come down to the developers. Certainly, Blizzard has the resources to update Hearthstone to accommodate the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra's square display. But I've been testing these foldables for the last seven years and things haven't improved. If Blizzard hasn't done anything by now, I doubt it's going to any time soon. I'd rather not leave it up to individual developers here.

What ends up happening, then, is I spend most of my time playing mobile games with the Fold 8 Ultra closed, and that kind of defeats the purpose of having a device that can unfold to a larger screen, doesn't it? Even then, while Samsung has vastly improved the aspect ratio of its foldables with the Fold 7 and Fold 8 Ultra, its outer display is still more narrow than a typical slab phone, which has its own problems.

On the surface, it'd seem like the iPhone Duo would have a lot of the same problems. Both its inner and outer displays have an odd 1.4:1 aspect ratio, which is smack dab in the middle of 16:9 and 4:3. The difference, though, is that Apple is famously strict with its developers. The company has already published guidelines for developing for the iPhone Duo , and the very first point is that developers should build apps to resize.

Now, there are definitely going to be some growing pains. It'll likely be a couple months before most major games have been adapted to the new form factor, but it's important to remember that Apple name-checked the iPad during its presentation. Most mobile games – including Hearthstone – natively support the various aspect ratios of Apple's tablets. Apple has had that guideline baked into its design documentation for years, and it's why apps largely work seamlessly between different Apple devices.

To be fair, Google also has similar guidelines in its developer documentation , but the difference is that Android has games as an exception to this rule. That's why its a gamble whether or not the game you want to play truly supports foldables. With the iPhone Duo, it does help that both the inner and outer display have the same aspect ratio, which should make resizing less of a technical hurdle. Regardless, I'm at least confident that Apple's foldable will have more games that just work on that inner display. Now, maybe I can finally play my silly little card games on a foldable without dealing with giant black bars.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Trump defends timing of $5,000 dividend announcement
articles.summary: President Trump defended the timing of his proposal to give every U.S. adult a $5,000 dividend — but only if Republicans maintain their majorities in the House and the Senate. “Why not just give the money now? If you have the money, why not give it now?” Fox News’s Laura Ingraham asked Trump in an…
articles.body:
President Trump defended the timing of his proposal to give every U.S. adult a $5,000 dividend — but only if Republicans maintain their majorities in the House and the Senate.

“Why not just give the money now? If you have the money, why not give it now?” Fox News’s Laura Ingraham asked Trump in an interview that will air in full Thursday night.

“Because the Democrats can’t do it, because for them it’s negative growth,” Trump responded. “But with us, it’s so positive.”

“We’re taking in $21 trillion. No country has ever taken in anywhere near that,” he continued. “It’s four or five times higher than the next, all because of the beautiful word that you and I love more than most others: tariffs.”

It’s unclear how the president would be able to implement such a move, given there are 270 million American adults, meaning the endeavor would cost the government roughly $1.35 trillion.

The proposal received immediate blowback following Trump’s announcement Wednesday night at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention.

In a social media post Thursday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) likened the proposal to bribery.

“Trump’s presidency is so failed and broken, he is resorting to trying to bribe the American people for their votes,” Schumer wrote.

Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) responded to the dividend, writing on social media, “Or maybe some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms.”

Vice President Vance defended the policy on Wednesday, suggesting tariff revenue could cover the costs.

“We’re taking in an extraordinary amount of revenue because the president of the United States is actually standing up to both foreign companies but also foreign countries who have been taking advantage of America’s workers for pretty much my entire life,” the vice president said.

“I don’t think it’s a controversial idea. It’s actually the president of the United States saying we’re all working together. We’re all on the same team, and if we continue to create wealth, that wealth is going to go back to the American people,” he continued.

articles.title: The Best iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max Cases
articles.body:
It’s September, so Apple just had a huge event , where it released an annual Pro phone update in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max . The standard iPhone 18 and follow-up to the iPhone Air didn’t make an appearance, though. Sorry, regular phone-havers, but you’ll have to wait a little while longer.

These new slabs of glass and metal are spendier than in years past , starting at $1,199 for the Pro and $1,299 for the larger Pro Max – a $100 price jump from their predecessors. Not that you wouldn’t have wanted to anyway, but protecting them is even more important. We’ve poked around, and picked out the best cases you can grab right now.

Your number one bet for an iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max case will be Apple’s first-party case. It’ll fit the best, and it supports both MagSafe and Apple’s Crossbody Strap and Wrist Strap accessories. The switch from FineWoven to TechWoven last year seems to have been the right call – by all accounts I’ve read, the cases have held up far better over the last year. The only things not to like about them, then, might be the look, as the colors haven’t gotten any more exciting this year. There’s also the feel; I’ve got issues with certain textures, and the TechWoven case gives me the creepy crawlies when I touch one.

The other thing to note is the price. Apple first-party cases don’t come cheap, and this year is no different. Expect to shell out $59 for the TechWoven case.

Dbrand’s collection of cool case designs comes straight to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. While you can certainly pick one that just has a single color, the company also has slick-looking options, like skins that look like X-rays of the interior of the phone or just the inside if you popped the back off. There are also cases with groovy inky splotches and the Sketch cases that look, well, like sketches.

The Grip Case is priced comparably to Apple’s first-party TechWoven cases, and most will run you $60, with some exceptions that are cheaper or more expensive (when not on sale).

Best Clear Case for iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

Dbrand’s Ghost Case is made up of a clear polycarbonate backing, complete with camera bump cover, and a dark edge. This take on the transparent case won’t ever yellow, Dbrand promises, because the part made with TPU, a material that usually darkens over time, is already dark and opaque. That also has the added advantage of feeling grippier in-hand.

The Ghost Case comes with an integrated magnetic ring for Qi2 wireless charging – the iPhone 18 Pro charges at up to 25W on a compatible charger. It’s on the pricey side, at $60, although right out of the gate, the company is selling it at a $10 discount.

Bullstrap has been my go-to for leather iPhone cases for years. Although its cases don’t tend to be quite as thin as Apple’s leather options were, it does offer the open-bottom design that I’ve always liked for using the swipe up gesture from the bottom of the phone. (There is a closed-bottom option, too.) The cases also feature clicky, metal buttons.

The cases don’t come cheap at $100 each, but the ones I’ve owned in the past have always felt like high-quality leather that develops a pleasing patina with time. For those who just can’t give up leather, Bullstrap’s is among the best.

Peak Design has made quality smartphone cases for years, particularly in the days before MagSafe, when the company offered its SlimLink modular accessory cases. The Everyday Case doesn’t support those, but it’s hard to see a need for them in a world filled with MagSafe accessories that accomplish the same thing.

It helps that the Peak Design Everyday Case, at $40, is the cheapest case on this list. You could absolutely find something at an even lower price, but you would be hard-pressed to find one that makes your phone feel as sturdy and pleasing to the touch as the cloth-backed Everyday Case.

Last month, Otterbox started straight-up listing its iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max cases as compatible with their 2026 replacements, and that’s as true today as it was then. According to Apple’s tech specs for the 18 Pro and 17 Pro models, they share the exact same dimensions.

A word of caution: there could be very subtle differences between the phones. Apple doesn’t give the exact measurements for the camera bump, for instance, and we don’t know if the buttons are in the exact same place. That could lead to tiny, annoying inconsistencies. Still, if you like the one you have and it’s not too beaten up, it might be worth trying it to see if you can save yourself a few bucks on a new case!

How to Pick an iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max Case

Whether you’re case-hunting for the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, the general advice I’d give is the same: Set your budget and needs, then look for options that fit it, from manufacturers you’ve trusted in the past. Given how much more durable phones are in 2026 than they were, say, 10 years ago, I tend to prioritize slimness and how they feel in my hand. But you might be more interested in a case that you could run over with a tank, or that offers extras like a kickstand or an integrated credit card slot.

If you don’t see or like the cases your favorite manufacturers have produced, your best bet is take a look at a few stories like this, figure out which cases, or at least which manufacturers, get mentioned the most. I’d only check the lists from sites you’ve heard of and that you feel you can trust. I do my best to pick cases from companies that haven’t done me wrong, but I certainly haven’t tried them all, so it’s best to get multiple opinions.

And if you’ve come here from the future, several months into the iPhone 18 Pro life cycle, you’ll probably be able to find a few actual reviews. The same thing applies, there: consider reviews from sources you trust. When I’m looking at them, I care most about people whose taste generally most closely matches my own.

Wes is a freelance writer (Freelance Wes, they call him) who has covered technology, gaming, and entertainment steadily since 2020 at Gizmodo, Tom's Hardware, Hardcore Gamer, and most recently, The Verge. Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.

articles.title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max get Variable Aperture as 'most important' camera feature: What it means for users
articles.summary: Tech News News: Apple has added variable aperture to the main camera on both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. This will offer users a physical way to control .
articles.body: Apple has added variable aperture to the main camera on both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. This will offer users a physical way to control how much light reaches the sensor for the first time on an iPhone.The feature sits alongside a new 48MP Fusion Main camera, a redesigned sensor and new Pro Controls. Apple says the six laser-cut blades inside the lens can move between four aperture settings, while the camera can also adjust the aperture automatically depending on the scene.That sounds like a minor hardware upgrade. But it is not. The lens opening affects exposure, depth of field, and how motion is captured, so giving the iPhone aperture control adds something software alone can't quite duplicate.Apple's description is straightforward: "iPhone 18 Pro has a new 48 megapixel fusion main camera with variable aperture for creative control that wasn't possible before," Apple said. "This is the most advanced camera we've ever made."Aperture is the part of a camera most phone users never seeAperture is simply the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. It is measured using f-numbers such as f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4.0.The lower the f-number, the wider the opening and the more light reaches the sensor. A wider aperture can therefore help in darker conditions. A narrower aperture lets in less light, but it also keeps more of the scene in focus.Most smartphone cameras use a fixed aperture. The lens has one opening, and the phone relies heavily on shutter speed, ISO, and computational photography to handle different lighting conditions.The iPhone 18 Pro changes that for its main camera. Its lens can open as wide as f/1.48 and then stop down to f/1.8, f/2.8 or f/4.0. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size.Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings rather than simply switching between two fixed positions.The camera can make that decision automatically. In a darker scene, it can open the aperture to f/1.48 and let in more light. In brighter conditions, it can narrow the opening.The useful bit is what happens when you take controlFor most people, the automatic system will do most of the work. The Camera app can choose an aperture based on the scene, just as it already decides on exposure and other settings.The difference is that iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max owners can also take control themselves.Apple's new Pro Controls let users manually change aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. A histogram can also be displayed to help judge exposure across a scene.That gives photographers another way to decide how a picture should look, instead of leaving every exposure decision to the camera.The most obvious example is depth of field. At a wider aperture such as f/1.48, the camera can produce more optical background blur when the subject is relatively close and the background is farther away.Stopping down to f/4.0 has the opposite effect. More of the scene can stay in focus, which can help with landscapes or group photos where people stand at different distances from the camera.That matters because a group shot can otherwise leave one person sharp while another, standing slightly farther away, falls outside the plane of focus. A narrower aperture gives the camera more room to keep those subjects in focus.It also gives photographers another option when deliberately introducing motion into an image. A narrower aperture reduces the amount of light entering the lens, making it easier to use a slower shutter speed when conditions are bright enough.It is not just about low lightThe obvious benefit of opening the aperture is light. Apple says the main camera can open to ƒ/1.48 for low-light photography, letting more light reach the sensor.That can give the camera more flexibility before it has to compensate by increasing ISO or slowing the shutter speed. In practical terms, that can help preserve detail and reduce noise, while a fast enough shutter can keep moving subjects sharp.But variable aperture is useful in the opposite direction too.In bright daylight, photographers sometimes want a slower shutter speed to create motion blur. That can be useful with moving water, people, or cars, and it also matters in video, where shutter speed is normally tied to frame rate.A fixed wide aperture can make that difficult in strong sunlight because too much light reaches the sensor even when the shutter is already operating at its fastest useful setting. Stopping the lens down gives the camera another way to reduce exposure.There are limits, though. A range ending at f/4.0 does not eliminate the need for neutral-density filters in every bright-light situation. Photographers who want long exposures in direct sunlight may still need an ND filter to cut the light further.The aperture is only on one cameraApple's implementation has an important limitation. The variable aperture is on the main 24mm camera. It does not extend across the entire rear camera system.The ultra-wide and telephoto cameras don't have the same variable-aperture mechanism. That means the new optical control is available only when shooting through the main lens.This is also why the feature should not be viewed as a replacement for the other cameras or for computational photography. Exposure, autofocus, HDR, noise reduction and image processing still determine much of the final photograph.The hardware simply gives the camera another physical variable to work with before those processes take over.Apple is adding more control to video tooAperture changes also feed into Apple's video features. The new Pro Controls work with video as well as photography, letting users manually adjust settings including aperture and shutter speed. That is especially relevant for people who want more predictable exposure rather than letting the phone change settings during recording.Apple has also added the ability to apply Cinematic effects after capture to videos recorded at up to 60 frames per second. That means users can make this adjustment after recording instead of committing to the effect while shooting.Time-lapse recording now supports 4K and Dolby Vision HDR, while Audio Mix has new algorithms designed to improve voice quality and isolate music.The combination is notable because Apple isn't presenting the variable aperture as an isolated camera specification. It is part of a broader attempt to give users more control over how photos and video are captured and processed.The idea isn't new to smartphonesApple is not the first phone maker to put a variable aperture in a smartphone. Samsung introduced a dual-aperture system with the Galaxy S9 series in 2018. That system switched between f/1.5 and f/2.4 depending on the lighting conditions.Huawei later introduced more flexible variable-aperture systems, while Xiaomi and Honor have also used the technology in flagship phones.The reason it has remained relatively uncommon is fairly simple: fitting a mechanical aperture mechanism into a smartphone camera adds complexity to an already tightly packed module.For years, phone makers instead concentrated on larger sensors, multiple cameras and computational photography. Those technologies can compensate for many of the limitations of a fixed aperture without adding moving parts to the lens.The iPhone 18 Pro's approach is therefore less about replacing computational photography than adding an optical control alongside it.The bigger camera change is the combinationThe variable aperture gets most of the attention, but Apple has made several other changes to the camera system.The 48MP Fusion Main camera uses a new sensor and a new computational imaging pipeline that Apple says produces sharper, more detailed images. Photographic Styles now include additional texture and grain controls, giving users more ways to change the look of their photos.Apple has also added persistent subject tracking for photos and video, letting the camera keep following a person even if they temporarily disappear behind someone else in a crowd.Another feature aimed at photographers is Apple Reference Image. When Reference mode is used, the camera captures signed sensor data that Private Cloud Compute turns into what Apple describes as an "unalterable reference image." You can then view the reference alongside the main photograph in the Photos app.The idea is to compare the original sensor-derived reference with the photograph and identify whether changes have been made. Apple says the feature is intended to address image authenticity, particularly for photographers and photojournalists.Apple is also adding metadata support and upcoming support for the SynthID standard to help identify images generated or edited with AI.What variable aperture actually changes for iPhone usersFor someone who simply opens the Camera app and takes pictures, it may not change much. The phone can choose the aperture automatically, just as it already handles most exposure decisions. For people who shoot deliberately, the change is more useful.A wider f/1.48 setting can help in darker scenes. Stopping down can keep more of a group or landscape in focus. Manual aperture control can also be combined with shutter-speed control to create particular motion effects.It can even produce optical effects that fixed-aperture smartphone cameras cannot reproduce in the same way, including changes in how bright points of light appear at narrower apertures.But four aperture settings don't turn the iPhone into a dedicated interchangeable-lens camera. The sensor remains small compared with most conventional cameras, and the amount of natural optical background blur depends heavily on the distance between the camera, subject, and background.For many portraits, Apple's computational Portrait mode will still produce a stronger and more controllable background-blur effect.The same is true for long exposures in bright daylight. The f/1.48-to-f/4.0 range gives photographers more room, but it does not remove the physical limits imposed by available light.That is probably the right way to look at the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture. It gives the camera one more physical control over exposure and focus, while the sensor and software continue to determine what ultimately reaches the screen.For casual users, most of that will happen automatically. For photographers and videographers who want to decide how the shot is captured, the four aperture settings and Pro Controls make the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max considerably more flexible than a fixed-aperture iPhone.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: How display of iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, is different from that of Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
articles.summary: Tech News News: Apple is finally jumping into the foldable phone game with the iPhone Duo, nearly 8 years after Samsung first brought folding smartphones to the world.
articles.body: Apple is finally jumping into the foldable phone game with the iPhone Duo, nearly 8 years after Samsung first brought folding smartphones to the world. The gap tells you a lot about how Apple has been careful in its approach to this format, choosing to wait and see. Foldables, in contrast, have matured over the years. When the South Korean behemoth launched its foldable lineup for the first time, the category felt more like an experiment than a mainstream product. The early foldables had visible fold lines, fragile screens and design compromises that made them feel more like a proof of concept than something built for real life. Over successive generations, Samsung steadily refined the formula, improving hinge mechanisms, reducing crease visibility and strengthening the display itself against daily wear and tear.This progress across the industry is essentially what allowed Apple to enter the space so much later with a more mature product. Rather than solving problems that plagued the first generation of foldables, Apple has had the advantage of building on lessons the industry has already learned, resulting in a device that arrives with far fewer of the early compromises foldable buyers once had to accept. But now that both companies have their foldables out in the market, let us take a closer look at how their screen technology actually compares.Apple iPhone Due vs Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8: Display specificationsBoth the iPhone Duo and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 use OLED display technology across their inner and outer screens – a now-standard choice for foldables. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold lineup has grown steadily over the years, with each generation typically bringing a marginally larger inner display alongside a wider, more usable outer cover screen. Apple’s iPhone Duo enters this same broad size category, aiming to offer a spacious inner display for multitasking and content viewingWhat sets Apple’s display apartApple has taken a distinctive approach with the iPhone Duo's display, built around what the company calls a nano-texture finish. This gives the screen a matte look that cuts down on glare and reflections, while also helping visually minimise the crease that naturally forms along a foldable's hinge area.
